extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate students studying real-variable analysis / advanced calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts of theorems, definitions, and constructive criteria from a textbook chapter on one-variable calculus: Taylor's theorem (integral remainder), power series and special functions, summability (Cesàro/Abel/Tauberian), and the Weierstrass approximation via approximate identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowest-order Taylor formulas and hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Three lowest-order expansions depending on hypotheses: (a) If f is merely continuous then f(x)=f(a)+o(1) as x→a. (b) If f is continuous on [a,x] and f' exists on (a,x) then f(x)=f(a)+f'(ξ)(x−a) for some a<ξ<x (Mean Value Theorem). (c) If f and f' are continuous on [a,x] then f(x)=f(a)+∫_a^x f'(t) dt (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This emphasizes that stronger regularity hypotheses give stronger remainder/conclusion forms. The three formulas illustrate increasing hypothesis strength: continuity → differentiability → integrability of derivative; use the weakest applicable form in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor's Theorem with integral remainder (Theorem 1.36)
rubrics_metrics.description:
Let n≥0, let a and x be points of R, and let f be complex-valued with n+1 continuous derivatives on the closed interval from a to x. Then
f(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x−a)/1!+...+f^{(n)}(a)(x−a)^n/n! + R_n(a,x),
with R_n(a,x) given by an explicit integral formula (integral remainder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem applies to real- or complex-valued functions. The full strength requires continuity of the appropriate derivatives on the closed interval. Use the integral formula for R_n(a,x) to estimate remainder and to decide when the infinite Taylor series converges to f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral remainder formula and ordering convention
rubrics_metrics.description: The remainder R_n(a,x) is given by an integral involving f^{(n+1)} (or f^{(n)} depending on indexing) and (x−t)^n / n!, with specific signs/forms depending on whether a≤x or x≤a. A convention (extending integrals when x<a) tidies the formula so one needn't assume a<x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating R_n use the integral form: R_n(a,x) = (1/n!) ∫_a^x (x−t)^n f^{(n+1)}(t) dt (with sign adjustments if x<a). The convention for integrals when x<a simplifies statements and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to complex-valued functions
rubrics_metrics.description: All the Taylor and remainder results extend to complex-valued functions by applying the real-valued versions to the real and imaginary parts separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use linearity: check integrability/continuity/differentiability of Re f and Im f to transfer results. Many proofs are the same componentwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radius of convergence and uniform convergence of power series (Theorem 1.37)
rubrics_metrics.description: A power series ∑ c_n z^n has a radius of convergence R. If 0≤R0<R then the series converges uniformly on the closed disk |z|≤R0 (hence uniformly on compact subsets inside the disk of convergence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Weierstrass M-test: pick R0<R and compare coefficients to a convergent majorant. This yields uniform convergence (and hence termwise operations) on every closed subdisk strictly inside the radius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term-by-term differentiation of power series (Corollary 1.38)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the power series ∑ c_n x^n converges for |x|<R (R>0) and its sum is f(x) for real x, then f has derivatives of all orders on |x|<R given by termwise differentiation; differentiated series also converge for |x|<R. In particular c_k = f^{(k)}(0)/k!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform convergence on closed subintervals permits termwise differentiation and iteration. Evaluate derivatives at center to recover coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of power series coefficients (Corollary 1.39)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two power series ∑ c_n x^n and ∑ d_n x^n both converge on |x|<R and have equal sums for real x with |x|<R, then c_n = d_n for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate termwise repeatedly and evaluate at the expansion center (e.g., 0) to equate coefficients; this follows from Corollary 1.38.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of exponential/sine/cosine via series
rubrics_metrics.description: Define exp z = ∑ z^n/n!, sin z = ∑_{n≥0} (−1)^n z^{2n+1}/(2n+1)!, cos z = ∑_{n≥0} (−1)^n z^{2n}/(2n)!. These series converge for all complex z (infinite radius) and hence define entire functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the radius is infinite, termwise differentiation and algebraic manipulation are valid globally. From the series one derives d/dx exp x = exp x, d/dx sin x = cos x, d/dx cos x = −sin x, and Euler's identity exp(i z)=cos z + i sin z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic and analytic consequences for exp, log, sin, cos
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences derived from series: exp(z+w)=exp z · exp w; exp conjugate = conjugate of exp; exp is strictly increasing on R with exp' = exp and inverse log on (0,∞) with derivative 1/x; trigonometric addition formulas sin(x+y)=sin x cos y + cos x sin y, cos(x+y)=cos x cos y − sin x sin y; definitions and basic properties of π via zeros of cos and resulting monotonicity/one-to-one intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use series algebra (Theorem 1.40 on product of series) and properties of derivatives to establish functional equations, monotonicity, and existence/uniqueness of inverse functions on the indicated intervals. Define π via the first positive zero of cos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication (Cauchy product) of power series (Theorem 1.40)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(z)=∑ a_n z^n and g(z)=∑ b_n z^n have radius of convergence > R>0, then the product f(z)g(z) equals ∑ c_n z^n with c_n = ∑_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n−k}; the product series converges for |z|<R and uniform convergence on smaller closed disks holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify by uniform convergence on |z|≤R0<R and regrouping (Weierstrass M-test). The formal multiplication (infinite distributive law) is valid inside the radius; watch for conditional convergence at the boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for Taylor series to equal function (remainder tends to zero)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has derivatives of all orders and the infinite Taylor series about a point converges at x, then the series sums to f(x) iff lim_{n→∞} R_n(a,x) = 0 where R_n is the integral remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To verify that the Taylor series equals f, estimate the integral remainder using bounds on higher derivatives; if the remainder tends to 0 for the x of interest, the series represents f at that x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial series expansion and validation technique (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any complex p, (1+x)^p has the binomial series ∑_{n≥0} (p choose n) x^n (valid for |x|<1). One validates the infinite series as the Taylor expansion by showing its sum f(x) satisfies a differential relation ((1+x)f'(x)=p f(x)) and matching an initial value to fix the multiplicative constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When remainder estimates are awkward, identify a candidate power series and verify it satisfies an ODE/functional equation that the target function must satisfy; use initial conditions to conclude equality on a neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cesàro summability: definition and arithmetic means
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sequence {s_n}, its Cesàro (arithmetic mean) sums are σ_n = (1/(n+1))∑_{k=0}^n s_k. If lim_{n→∞} σ_n exists (in C) the sequence is Cesàro summable to that limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cesàro summability can assign limits to sequences that do not converge (example: s_n = (−1)^n is not convergent but Cesàro summable to 0 because σ_n oscillates but tends to 0). Use Cesàro means when partial sums oscillate but average out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between ordinary convergence and Cesàro sums (Abelian fact, Theorem 1.47)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sequence {s_n} converges to s then its Cesàro means σ_n converge to s as well (convergence implies Cesàro summability with the same limit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses splitting the average into a fixed initial block and a tail close to s; the contribution of the fixed block vanishes as n→∞. This is an example of an Abelian theorem: one mode of convergence implies another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abel summability and Abel's Theorem (Theorem 1.48)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given partial sums s_n = ∑_{k=0}^n a_k, form the Abel sums σ(r)=∑_{n≥0} s_n r^n for 0≤r<1. If s_n → s as n→∞ then lim_{r↑1} σ(r) = s (the Abel sums tend to the ordinary sum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express σ(r) in terms of the s_k and use manipulations analogous to the Cesàro argument; Abel's theorem shows that ordinary convergence implies Abel summability to the same limit (another Abelian theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tauberian conclusion for nonnegative coefficients (Proposition 1.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {a_k} are nonnegative reals and the series (or its Abel sums) is Abel summable to s, then the sequence of partial sums s_n = ∑_{k=0}^n a_k actually converges to s (i.e., Abel summability implies ordinary convergence for nonnegative terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotonicity and nonnegativity permit interchanging limits (monotone convergence argument); this is a basic Tauberian-type result where an extra hypothesis (nonnegativity) gives the converse direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition on rate control via boundedness (Proposition 1.50 — summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {s_n} are partial sums of a series and their Cesàro sums converge, then boundedness of the sequence {n a_n} (or related boundedness hypotheses) implies ordinary convergence of the partial sums, and the rate of convergence can be bounded in terms of the bound on {n a_n} and the Cesàro convergence rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a quantitative Tauberian-type statement useful in applications (e.g., pointwise convergence of Fourier series): boundedness of n·a_n controls how Cesàro convergence translates into ordinary convergence and provides uniformity/rate information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass Approximation Theorem idea via approximate identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Any continuous complex-valued function on a bounded interval [a,b] is the uniform limit of polynomials. The constructive device is convolution of f with a polynomial 'approximate identity' φ_n to produce smooth (in this construction, polynomial) approximants that converge uniformly to f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement by choosing polynomial φ_n supported in a small interval with total integral 1 and most mass concentrated near 0; the convolution f * φ_n is as smooth as the smoother of f and φ_n. Taking φ_n polynomials yields polynomial approximants to f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties required of an approximate identity (construction lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: φ_n(x)=c_n(1−x^2)^n on [−1,1] with c_n chosen so ∫ φ_n =1. The φ_n satisfy: (i) ∫ φ_n = 1 (normalization), (ii) φ_n(x)≥0 and supported in [−1,1], (iii) for any δ>0, sup_{|x|≥δ} φ_n(x) → 0 as n→∞ (mass concentrates near 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three properties ensure that convolution with φ_n approximates a continuous function uniformly: normalization preserves values on average, nonnegativity prevents cancellations, and mass concentration forces the average to be dominated by values near each point.
